title: Core types: outcome values, big-int quantities, Die construction
details: The foundation. An outcome value type following Python's rules (docs/semantics.md: bool is an int and merges with 1, str, tuple, float, Fraction; Python's ordering, raising on incomparable types). Big-integer quantities (pick the crate, note why in NOTES.md). A Die: sorted (outcome, quantity) items exactly as icepool's Counts keeps them (population/base.py, population/die.py __new__, collection/counts.py, creation_args.py). Wire encoding/decoding (harness/core/encode.py) in program/. Make the grammar nodes d, die, weights fuzz clean and mark them ported. Design the core so later tasks (arithmetic, map, pools, evaluators, PyO3, WASM) fit: read docs/ANALYSIS.md first and write the module layout you chose into NOTES.md.

title: Arithmetic and comparison operators
details: Die-die and die-scalar binary operators (+ - * / // % ** << >> & | ^, < <= > >=) and unary ones (- + ~ abs, round/trunc/floor/ceil), with Python's mixed-type semantics, bool-as-int, tuple concatenation, int/int -> float for /. Port binary_operator / unary_operator from population/die.py and base.py. Existing nodes add, sub, mul, neg, lt, ge: make them fuzz clean and ported. Add grammar nodes for every other operator, including scalar-on-the-left forms (3 - die), division by zero (raises), and float outcomes.

title: map, mixtures, Reroll; reroll/filter/split/clip/truncate
details: Die.map / icepool.map without repeat (map_tools/function.py, core_impl.py): callables come from harness/catalogue (named functions with a Python and a Rust side; start with ~15: add_k, clamp, read_roll from khepri, is_even, swap/tuple ops, ones that return a Die, ones that return Reroll, star-style multi-argument ones). Results that are Dice are mixed with weighted_lcm exactly (creation_args.py, math.py). Extra Die arguments to map (cartesian product). Then reroll (with depth and 'inf'), filter, split, clip, truncate, and the Die([die1, die2]) / weighted mixture constructors. Grammar nodes for all of it.

title: Repeated sums (@), explode, Again in depth mode
details: n @ die with int and Die n, _sum_all caching, the den**(max|n|-|n|) scaling (die.py). explode (which outcomes, depth, end) via the Again expression in depth mode (population/again.py evaluate_agains_using_depth): port Again as a closed Rust enum, depth mode only for now (count mode is a Phase S task). matmul node to ported; add explode and again nodes.

title: Pool, keep tuples, popping

title: Multiset evaluation driver and built-in evaluators

title: Keep counts and count multipliers beyond i64
details: Left over from K6b. Python keep counts are unbounded ints: d6.pool([2**70, 1]).sum(), pool * 2**63, keep tuples whose keep_size passes 2**63 (two counts of 2**62), Die.keep with such counts. The port refuses them cleanly today (program/pool.rs exact_int 'not a 64-bit int', keep_size / multiply_counts overflow -> Unsupported 'keep counts beyond 64 bits'; facade: NotImplementedError), it never wraps. Doing it means a count type wider than i64 through the whole multiset stack: keep_tuple.rs (make/compose/pop), pool.rs (keep_tuple, Count::Int / Count::Tuple yielded by MultisetSource::pop), deal.rs, compound_keep.rs, operator/* (counts arithmetic, MultisetKeep), evaluator/* (sum multiplies outcome by count, size, product_of_counts, poker, keep ...), program/expression.rs and the facade's conversions (about 300 i64 sites). Suggested shape: a `Count` newtype with an i64 fast path and checked arithmetic falling back to IBig, so ordinary evaluations do not slow down (check with the long gate's timings). Add generators that now and then produce counts near and beyond 2**63 (pool_keep, die_pool sequences, pool_mul, die_keep), fuzz clean through icepool-run and crates/icepool-py/run-facade.sh, with fixtures.

title: Built-in evaluators over tuple counts (MultiDeal and user tuple sources) on the core
details: FACADE-AUDIT item 4 (S5c split it off): with a MultisetTupleSource input (a MultiDeal, a user tuple source) or tuple counts from operators, the built-in evaluators (sum without map, size, product_of_counts, empty, expand, keep, the poker ones, all_counts, largest_straight*, count_subset, the seven comparisons) run through evaluate_host callbacks in the facade (correct, slower) and say Unsupported in icepool-run (program layer; the generators avoid them). Python has no special case: its arithmetic just runs on the tuple count, case by case, e.g. SumEvaluator `outcome * count` repeats a tuple (int outcome) and `state + ...` concatenates; `count == 1` is False; ExpandEvaluator `(outcome,) * count` is TypeError; SizeEvaluator `0 + count` TypeError; ProductOfCounts `1 * count` is the tuple, then tuple * tuple TypeError; EmptyEvaluator `count == 0` is False. Port each built-in's next_state / initial_state / final_outcome for Count::Tuple in the core (as S4f did for operators: crates/icepool-core/src/operator/mod.rs next_state_tuple), with states as Values where they stop being ints; let builtin_spec in python/icepool/evaluator/evaluator_rust.py name them for tuple sources too (evaluate / rust_call_tree currently refuse builtins when _tuple_source); add grammar coverage (multi_deal / tuple_op_evaluate generators picking built-ins over tuple counts), fuzz clean through icepool-run and run-facade.sh, fixtures, facade cases.

title: argsort and lexi evaluators over tuple counts on the core
details: S5d ported the other built-in evaluators' next_state for tuple counts (MultisetEvaluator::next_state_values / reads_sizes, see NOTES S5d). ArgsortEvaluator (drop / left / right), ArgsortGroupedEvaluator and LexiComparisonEvaluator still say Unsupported for a tuple count or size in icepool-run, and the facade calls them back (builtin_spec returns None with tuple_counts). Python's arithmetic runs on the tuples case by case: argsort drop compares `count > max_count` (TypeError) but with limit <= len(state) never looks at counts; left/right compute `min(count, limit - len(state))` or `count` then `append_count > 0`; grouped short-circuits on the limit before `count > 0`; lexi's initial_state compares tuple sizes in reverse order and next_state does `max(left, 0)`. Port them over Values, let builtin_spec name them for tuple sources, add them to builtin_evaluate's generator (or a sibling node), fuzz through icepool-run and run-facade.sh, fixtures, facade cases.

title: Reflected multiset operators with an Again or Deck left operand, and mx_str of a non-expression

title: Robustness: recursion depth guard (no segfaults)
details: Deeply nested Vectors segfault through the Python facade where Python raises RecursionError: `t=1; for i in range(5000): t=Vector([t])` then `t+t` (also Die([t]), ==, str at depth 100000). Recursion without a depth guard in crates/icepool-py/src/convert.rs from_py/to_py and recursive Value ops/eq/format (value/ops.rs, vector.rs, format.rs). Add a depth limit everywhere user data drives recursion (conversion, Value ops, eq, hash, ordering, formatting, expression trees) that raises RecursionError (Python) / a proper error (Rust, JS). Audit every other recursion on user-controlled depth. Add fixtures/tests for each. Background: docs/reviews/2026-10-17-library-review.md (the three library-wide reviews: robustness, performance, code quality). Parity with the oracle stays absolute for native and Python builds.

title: Robustness: no aborts or traps on huge inputs; panic guards at every entry point
details: `{"op":"d","sides":8589934592}` aborts the process (allocation failure, uncatchable); sides=2**63-1 panics (function.rs:22, capacity overflow); die_sequence with huge rolls does vec![die; rolls] (program/collection.rs:64); JS d(2n**63n-1n) is a wasm trap. Move the size checks the Python facade does today into the core (d(), cartesian_product, every with_capacity / vec![x; n] / repeat sized by user input: audit all of them), returning a proper overflow/memory error; use try_reserve where sizes are large; cap below what wasm32's 4 GB address space can hold. Then catch_unwind (or equivalent) around every WASM export and PyO3 entry point as a backstop, converting panics to proper exceptions, and make sure thread-locals/RefCells (HANDLES, VARS) cannot stay poisoned after one. Background: docs/reviews/2026-10-17-library-review.md (the three library-wide reviews: robustness, performance, code quality). Parity with the oracle stays absolute for native and Python builds.

title: Robustness leftovers: pool denominators on wasm32, direct WASM exports after a trap
details: Left by R2 (see NOTES.md "Huge sizes and panics (R2)"): (1) pool.rs denominator() is den**count for up to 2**24 dice with no check_pow (infallible today): on wasm32 a die with a 129+-bit denominator in a huge pool can pass the 256 MiB cap and trap; make it fallible or bound it. (2) The WASM exports run() and calculate() (run-wasm.mjs, khepri's worker) are not wrapped like js/core.js wasm(): after a trap the shadow stack pointer and recursion state are not restored (run-wasm.mjs reloads the instance; khepri's worker does not). Give them the same recovery (e.g. a small JS helper shipped with the package, or document reloading).

title: Robustness: Ctrl-C and the GIL during long computations
details: `(d(100).pool(400).highest(200).sum()).mean()` ignores SIGINT for over a minute (the oracle raises KeyboardInterrupt in 0.2 s), and the GIL is held throughout, blocking other Python threads. Add an interrupt hook the core polls in long loops (evaluator DP, convolutions, map(repeat), Markov elimination, big constructions), e.g. a `&dyn Fn() -> Result<()>` or a cancellation token in the evaluation context; PyO3 implements it with py.check_signals(). Release the GIL (allow_threads/detach) around pure-Rust work that makes no Python callbacks. Test with a subprocess sending SIGINT, and a second Python thread making progress meanwhile. Background: docs/reviews/2026-10-17-library-review.md (the three library-wide reviews: robustness, performance, code quality). Parity with the oracle stays absolute for native and Python builds.

title: Robustness: leaks
details: Investigate the possible leak: 20k iterations of d(6).map(lambda o, big=big: o) + pool(3).sum() grew maxrss 1.7 MB vs 0.77 MB in the oracle. Run long tracemalloc / RSS loops; callbacks held as Py<PyAny> inside Rust Arcs are invisible to Python's cycle GC: implement __traverse__/__clear__ where PyO3 objects can hold Python references. JS: handles are freed only by FinalizationRegistry; add explicit dispose (Symbol.dispose / release()) and document it. Add a leak regression test for both. title: Robustness: cycles through icepool_rs objects that share core data
details: Left by R4 (NOTES.md "Cycles and the collector (R4)"): an icepool_rs object reports a Python object to the cycle collector only if no other object shares the core data holding it (icepool_core::ownership; a shared one must never be reported). So a garbage cycle that contains two Python wrappers sharing core data is still not collected on the Rust backend: a CompoundKeepGenerator and its _inner_generators (RsCompoundKeep's sources share the inner pools' dice; check with gc.get_referents(x._rs) == []), a die and a pool of it both reachable only from the cycle, a facade object and its cached _rs-derived objects. Fix the structural ones the way RsDeal / RsMultiDeal were fixed (hold the Python wrapper of the shared part, build the core value per call), starting with CompoundKeep; add each to CYCLES in crates/icepool-py/tests/test_leaks.py. Parity with the oracle stays absolute.

title: Design: typed core, Rust API, error types, crate layout, JS/TS API, production builds
details:
Write docs/design/library-architecture.md BEFORE any of the C tasks change code. Decide and specify, with code sketches:
(1) Outcome trait: Ord + Hash + Clone for typed outcomes (i64, tuples, ...); Python's fallible comparison and semantics live in a Value-only layer (e.g. Value implements a separate PyOutcome/fallible trait, or the generic algorithms are written against a small trait both satisfy) - the core must not require py_lt/py_eq.
(2) How evaluators (poker, keep, basic, lexi, argsort, comparison), map, explode/Again, formatting become generic so Die<i64> users get them; Value's Python behaviour as one implementation.
(3) Error types: domain-named variants (EmptyDie, Incomparable, ConflictingOrder, Overflow, ...) in core; the Python exception mapping lives in icepool-py and the runner.
(4) Public Rust API: std::ops on Die, typed constructors (d(6) for i64, from ranges/slices/weights), Display, iterators, curated re-exports, everything else pub(crate); what docs.rs shows.
(5) Crate layout: icepool-core (the library, no serde_json, no runner), icepool-py (Python bindings), icepool-wasm (JS/TS bindings), and a separate harness crate (e.g. icepool-harness: JSON program runner, icepool-run binary, fixtures test) used only by tests. Host-callback traits consolidated in one core module. Feature flags, if any.
(6) The JS/TypeScript API: its own idiomatic API, as close to Python icepool as possible (classes Die, Pool, Deck, MultisetEvaluator..., method names mirroring icepool's, camelCase or snake_case decision, operators as methods, BigInt quantities, iteration protocols, callbacks, evaluator subclassing in JS), NOT a JSON-op RPC. Mapping table Python API -> TS API.
(7) Documentation plan for each binding: Rust (rustdoc + crate-level guide), Python (same docs as upstream, plus what differs), JS/TS (its own docs: a guide + generated API reference, e.g. TypeDoc, with examples).
(8) Production builds: the Python wheel and the npm package contain no tests, fixtures, runner or harness code; how scripts/check-production.sh verifies it (the gate runs it once it exists).
(9) Migration order for tasks C1-C8, keeping the gate green at every step (the harness crate keeps driving the oracle comparison throughout).
Keep it concise and decisive. No production code changes in this task; it may add tasks or refine C1-C8 details in tasks.json. Background: docs/reviews/2026-10-17-library-review.md (the three library-wide reviews: robustness, performance, code quality). Parity with the oracle stays absolute for native and Python builds.
